A cargo ship with Russian military connections was still burning late on Saturday as it sat at anchor in Finnish waters, with Finland leading the rescue operation after what it said was likely a Ukrainian attack.
Finnish authorities said Russian vessels might eventually tow the wreckage back to Russia .
The 16-member crew of the Sparta II abandoned the vessel for lifeboats before transferring to a nearby Russian ship, and is now heading back to Russia, Finnish Border Guard Commander Ilja Iljin told public broadcaster Yle late on Saturday.
The ship was struck by drones and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, in an incident Finland said was likely an attack by Ukraine, and it later drifted into Finnish waters.
Finland's Defence Forces said the vessel, which was bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad , was damaged in international waters west of Russia's Gogland island, corroborating an earlier account from Russian officials.
Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia's northwest Leningrad region this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of the Baltic region, leading to fears that the war was affecting NATO territory.
"It is likely that Ukraine... is behind (the attack)," Finnish armed forces spokesperson Aki-Mauri Huhtinen told a press conference, adding it was not clear why the ⁠vessel had been targeted.
Mikko Simola, commander of the Gulf of Finland Coast Guard, said a Russian helicopter was suspected of briefly violating Finnish airspace during the rescue operation.
Helsinki said it had introduced temporary aviation and maritime restrictions in the ‌eastern Gulf of Finland to protect civilians and allow authorities to operate if drones needed to be intercepted.
"The war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas. Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight ‌against the aggressor," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said on X.
Sweden's Defence Minister Pal Jonson said Swedish combat aircraft, operating under ‌Finnish command, took part in safeguarding Finland's and NATO's territorial integrity following the incident.
Finland and Sweden are NATO's newest member states, joining the military alliance in 2023 and 2024, respectively, in response to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"The consequences of fighting Russia's aggression have reached the Baltic Sea. Another signal for the aggressor to stop. But nothing will stop us from supporting ⁠Ukraine," Estonia's Prime Minister Kristen Michal wrote on X.
Estonia's government said it had sent a navy vessel to assist in the rescue operation, including firefighting and pollution response.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Russia's embassy in Helsinki did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The vessel is subject to US sanctions and is linked to Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika, according to the US Treasury Department.
According to the company's website, Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Defence Ministry.
"At the moment, there is no confirmed information about what cargo is on board, but it cannot be ruled out that there is military materiel on board," Iljin of the Finnish Border Guard said.
Leningrad region Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said on Telegram that a cargo vessel had been attacked ‌by two drones in international waters about 3 nautical miles from Russia's border.
Drozdenko also said 80 drones had been shot down over the Leningrad ​region overnight.
Finland's military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during a wave ‌of Ukrainian drone attacks on the Leningrad region.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said ⁠the incident posed no threat to supplies to the region.
Kaliningrad, which lies between Poland and Lithuania, has periodically been a flashpoint between Russia and ⁤NATO and the European Union.
Russia has previously described attacks on its commercial vessels outside its territorial waters as acts of terrorism and maritime piracy.
The Sparta II is a 121-metre (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Oboronlogistika ‌that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to LSEG ​data.
The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between ‌Finland and Estonia that extends east to St Petersburg.
Gogland lies in ​the eastern Gulf of Finland.

SHENZHEN, China — Donald Trump met Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a villa in southern China, an unprecedented gathering of a U.S. president with Washington’s chief geopolitical rivals bent on undermining American power.
The meeting, conceived not by policymakers but by Trump and Putin, had a fractured agenda, with each leader coming to the table with divergent interests and different stakes.
As they dispersed to their capitals, the presidents had few tangible gains to show for a summit hastily assembled in a matter of weeks, bypassing the months of groundwork that typically underpin diplomatic breakthroughs.
But the image of Trump standing alongside Putin and Xi — then sitting alone with the two of them, at a great round table in a cacophonous hall — was itself the culmination of a decade of his foreign policy thinking, a great-man theory of diplomacy that has broken with American tradition, elevating authoritarian leaders over democratic allies.
The U.S. president appeared subdued, thanking Xi and Putin before turning to journalists.
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” he said, arguing he had a “special responsibility” to maintain dialogue with adversarial world powers. “We are really making history.”
Unlike at Yalta in 1945, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Josef Stalin famously gathered to shape the postwar order, the American leader was not at the center of these photographs. That place of honor belonged to Xi, the host, who presided over the gathering at a remote retreat outside the city.
It was a portrait of a nation asserting its place among the world’s superpowers — the very image Beijing had sought in agreeing to host the extraordinary gathering.
“History tells us that when great powers are at peace, the world is secure,” Xi said. “When great powers clash, the world is in chaos.”
The competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that harken back to the famous Yalta conference of 1945.
But if any substantive understandings were reached behind closed doors, none of them were released to the public.
The summit’s pageantry fit a familiar pattern for Trump, who has repeatedly staged headline-grabbing encounters with controversial leaders only to walk away empty-handed. Three high-stakes meetings with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his first term failed to meaningfully shift relations between Washington and Pyongyang, and a meeting with Putin in Anchorage last year likewise failed to generate progress toward ending Russia’s war in Ukraine.
This time, the spectacular gathering lasted just an hour and a half, and produced only a readout of four points of agreement, broadly committing to work to uphold international security, minimize nuclear risks, increase petroleum output and, most specifically, overhaul the United Nations and the International Criminal Court, which it said “must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
The court has a warrant outstanding for Putin’s arrest.
Putin framed the trilateral meeting as one of equals, elevating a Russian Federation that has been economically and militarily devastated, and ostracized from the international community, over its war against Ukraine. Russian state media highlighted Xi’s decision to place Putin to his right throughout the summit as a gesture of honor.
“I am convinced that Russia, China and the United States, our peoples, are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world,” Putin said, “if they cooperate constructively as partners on the basis of mutual respect, equality and a balance of interests.”
The Russian leader appeared almost giddy throughout the day’s meetings, and upon departing Shenzhen for the airport, escorted personally by Xi to his car, was heard saying, “I don’t think anyone ever expected everything to go so well.”
“The trilateral summit was a giant gift to Putin. It put him on a stage where he does not belong,” Michael McFaul, a former U.S. ambassador to Russia now at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, told The Times. “The photo of that meeting will be seen throughout the world, making it look like Putin is a respected leader of a great power. What did Americans get in return? Nothing, absolutely nothing.”
The unusual summit comes just weeks after Trump suffered a generational rebuke in the midterm elections and as he remains bogged down in a war with Iran, which threatened to erupt in a new round of hostilities in the coming days.
Publicly, Trump framed the gathering as an effort to curb nuclear proliferation. Yet instead of advancing a trilateral nonproliferation agreement among the world’s three largest nuclear powers, Putin offered a message of defiance, sending nuclear-capable bombers to nearby Vietnam a day before the summit in a rare deployment. China, meanwhile, rebuffed calls to slow down its breakneck nuclear buildup currently dwarfed by America’s arsenal.
The Trump administration let the last remaining U.S. arms control agreement with Russia expire earlier this year.
“Despite the talk of denuclearization by the Trump administration, no staff members prepped the president to meaningfully discuss this topic with Putin or Xi, who are unwilling partners for restraints and guardrails,” said Jennifer Hong, senior director of the Institute for Indo-Pacific Security.
Instead, Trump’s focus seems to have turned to ensuring nonproliferation not among world powers, but in the Middle East — the main justification he has given for launching war against the Islamic Republic this year.
“We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said at the start of the meeting.
Putin had hoped the summit would secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine — a prospect that Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, took seriously as the meeting was about to begin.
“Big countries always think that they can make decisions about the future of all the world,” Zelensky told NBC News. “It’s a huge mistake.”
Sitting alongside Xi, Trump said the two of them were looking to “help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine” and “would like to see it ended.”
Few independent analysts believe Putin is interested in ending the war in its current state. But at the trilateral engagement, Trump suggested Zelensky was responsible for Moscow’s continued attempts at conquest. “Things are happening,” Trump said. “I think that [Putin] and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war.”
The meetings were Trump’s first with Putin since their summit last year in Alaska, a gathering that failed to produce a breakthrough in the Republican president’s attempts to bring an end to the deadliest conflict in Europe since World War II.
Trump met individually with  Putin and Xi ahead of the trilateral gathering despite White House officials insisting before the trip that a direct meeting with Putin was not on the agenda.
“Who is he? He’s my friend,” Trump said, walking toward Putin with an outstretched hand.
“We have had a great relationship for many years. We’ve known each other for a long time,” Trump added. “And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start.”
A Russian diplomat attending the conference with Putin told reporters that Trump and Putin together are “committed to a peaceful resolution to the Ukrainian conflict, though the Europeans are clearly trying to stand in the way.”
European officials have been wary of the Shenzhen summit, warning against the future of Ukraine being negotiated without Ukrainians present. A Chinese official told The Times they would have been welcome to attend, but no invitation was formally extended.

articles.title_orig: Developers have released the Leonida tool for natively running Grand Theft Auto VI on PC.
articles.title_zh: Developers have released the Leonida tool for natively running Grand Theft Auto VI on PC.
articles.content_orig:
Leonida, an open source project aimed at statically recompiling the console version of Grand Theft Auto VI for Xbox Series X into a native OS application, has appeared on the GitHub platform. WindowsSince the console processor uses the x86-64 architecture, the authors of the initiative translate the console system calls into the PC environment, and translate the compiled RDNA2 graphics programs into the SPIR-V format for operation via the API. VulkanThe project is distributed under the GPL-3.0 license and does not contain any copyrighted game files, encryption keys, or executable modules. To build the port, the user will need an unpacked copy of version 1.0.2.1 of the game, from which the utilities will automatically extract the necessary assets and generate shaders locally on the computer.
At this stage the game does not launch yet, as the developers lack an executable file to complete the work on the loader and the D3D12 graphics layer for VulkanHowever, the toolkit already successfully extracts and converts all 26 game shaders to SPIR-V, as well as exports 503D models to OBJ format, textures to DDS, and audio tracks to Ogg Opus or WAV. Building the project independently on a PC requires certain software and hardware requirements.
The automated build script automatically finds the game folder on local drives using the MicrosoftGame.Config configuration, checks for the presence of the required components, and saves the finished result in the user's documents directory. WindowsThe process of resource extraction and shader validation is supported on Linux, where the executable loader can be launched via Wine or Proton. The project's repository already has over 8,2 stars and 147 contributors, who continue to refine the translation of graphics commands and the emulation of 64-thread shader groups for NVIDIA and Intel graphics cards.

articles.title_orig: South Korea’s Education Minister Resigns Over Anti-A.I. Cheating Rules
articles.title_zh: South Korea’s Education Minister Resigns Over Anti-A.I. Cheating Rules
articles.content_orig:
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.
A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.
Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

articles.title_orig: Turkey's final draft at UN climate talks doesn't mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming
articles.title_zh: Turkey's final draft at UN climate talks doesn't mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming
articles.content_orig:
The fate of United Nations climate talks in Turkiye is hanging in the balance as the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31) co-presidents, Australia and Turkiye, struggle to secure consensus on a deal to advance the fight against climate change, raising ⁠⁠the prospect of no deal being reached.
The new draft of the deal was released on Sunday, two days after the conference in Antalya was scheduled to end.
If approved, it would acknowledge for the first time that global ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠warming is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) threshold that countries had sought to preserve, while calling for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse the overshoot.
The draft omits mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say are driving climate change, an issue that has been at the centre of frictions at the talks. Instead, it includes language referring to ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌a previous COP at which governments had agreed to transition away from oil, gas and coal.
“We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon,” COP31 President Murat Kurum told a plenary session early on Sunday.
Kurum, who is also Turkiye’s environment minister, said the conference would reconvene later on Sunday morning to approve the deal.
Other delegations at the venue, where catering outlets and exhibits have already been dismantled, were less sure.
French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said the proposal was a “backward” step. “Time is ticking and we are not there yet,” she said.
An earlier draft had provoked strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels, the largest contributors to climate change.
Environmental group 350.org said it was disappointed by the continued omission in the new draft, as well as its encouragement of carbon-removal technologies.
“Carbon capture is one of the biggest scams of the overshoot era and our leaders are on ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠the verge of falling for it,” said Sara Shaw, the group’s campaigns and networks ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠director, referring to the practice of trapping carbon dioxide before it reaches the atmosphere.
Observers at the closed-door talks said Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producing nations had pushed hard to keep fossil fuels out of the ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠text and carbon removal in.
A representative of the Saudi delegation declined to comment.
Kurum said he ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠believed concerns around fossil fuels had ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌been addressed, as had those ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌around helping developing countries finance their adaptation to climate change.
The new ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌text followed intensive consultations between Australia, which is ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌leading the talks; Turkiye, which is hosting the meeting; and nearly 200 delegations from many of the world’s richest, poorest, largest and smallest nations.
The summit’s agreement is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which drives heatwaves, floods and other disasters.
An opening draft from Australia on Monday called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels. A slimmer version on Thursday removed every mention of them after Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers objected.
Key issues that slowed the agreement included how much effort countries should make to wean themselves off fossil fuels, such as coal, oil and gas.
Other issues included whether to encourage industrial carbon capture and storage of pollutants, as well as whether ramping up electricity generation should only be done with renewables, such as wind and solar, or also involve other sources such as natural gas and coal.
To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut fossil fuel emissions.
The two-week talks in the Turkish city were due to end on Friday.
In a letter sent on Saturday to this year’s cohosts, Turkiye and Australia, 100 civil society groups warned that they were “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs” the UN has ever held.
The letter stated there were only hours left “to save this COP from becoming a low point of three decades of climate negotiations”.
In the lead-up to these talks, the UN said the world would likely blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial temperatures.

A mathematician working for the AI company Anthropic claims to have proved the Riemann hypothesis – the most famous unsolved problem in the mathematical world – using the large language model Claude .
The hypothesis, first proposed in 1859 by Germany’s Bernhard Riemann, claims that the location of prime numbers along the number line are not random, but are instead determined by a meaningful order.
It is of importance to mathematicians because it links the distribution of prime numbers to a precise pattern.
The hypothesis was identified by influential mathematician David Hilbert in 1900 as one of his 23 mathematical challenges for the 20th century.
In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute offered a $1 million reward for anyone who could prove the hypothesis.
Anthropic ’s Dr Levent Alpöge claimed the breakthrough in a statement posted to his website on Friday.
“I believe I have, working with Claude , discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” he wrote.
“It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.”
Dr Alpöge has released a version of the proof which is written in the computer code Lean, which is used to verify the mathematical correctness of arguments.
Experts will now need to examine whether the work is properly coded and if the hypothesis has, indeed, been proved.
Dr Alpöge, who holds dual United States and Turkish citizenship, has an MA from Harvard , a Master of Advanced Studies from the University of Cambridge , and a PhD from Princeton .
In July, he made headlines when he posted a counterexample to the famous Jacobian conjecture, a well-known problem in the field of algebraic geometry.
Like his work on the Riemann hypothesis, he had used Claude to make the discovery.
“hello there the jacobian conjecture is false thanx to my close friend akhil for asking about it and my other close friend fable for working during the world cup final,” he posted on X (formerly Twitter).
Dr Alpöge’s statement on the Riemann hypothesis on Friday was slightly longer and more erudite.
“I hope the argument provides a glimpse towards the miracles that lie ahead, and shows us the joy and wonder we are about to find in the simplest things,” he wrote.

articles.title_orig: Why more families in Hull are choosing home education
articles.title_zh: Why more families in Hull are choosing home education
articles.content_orig:
Aimee believes removing her nine-year-old son from school has helped him get "the sparkle back in his eyes".
George is non-verbal with profound and multiple learning disabilities and while he attended a specialist school in Hull, Aimee felt his needs were not being met.
In January, George became one of more than 1,000 children being educated at home in the city, according to a council report – a figure that has grown from 380 in 2022.
"We've just found George is a lot more relaxed, a lot more settled and he's just happier," Aimee says.
Education experts, teachers and the city council say there are a variety of reasons why home education numbers are increasing in Hull, including the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic, educational philosophy and greater awareness of special educational needs and disabilities.
Aimee, 31, says George had a "fantastic" first four years at the school, but this changed as he got older and moved up a class.
"[Home education] wasn't a path we wanted to take when he first in the school – he was happy and it was great.
"We just felt like, sometimes, George was being treated as a number."
She says George has more flexibility at home, where he still sees specialists in occupational therapy, physiotherapy and speech and language. He also has cooking sessions.
Prof Richard Woolley, head of the school of education at the University of Hull, suggests an increase in awareness of SEND is among "complex and varied" reasons why more families are educating at home.
According to figures from the Department for Education (DFE) for autumn 2025, 16% of children in home education had an additional SEND requirement.
Woolley says: "Now we talk about different needs, we talk about diagnosis, we talk about neurodiversity in a way that we wouldn't have done, five, even 10, years ago.
"It's become much more a part of our awareness as a society. We understand children's needs much more fully."
However, the professor says mainstream schools are "amazingly well-equipped" for supporting SEND children, with knowledge and expertise that "is the best that it ever has been".
The latest published figures from the DFE show there were 380 home-educated children in Hull in the autumn of 2022 and 830 in the same period of 2025.
However, a report compiled for a Hull City Council scrutiny panel , in October this year, stated the number being educated at home reached 1,086 in the year to March 2026.
The rise reflects the national picture. The DFE states 126,000 children in England were educated at home in the autumn of 2025, compared with 86,200 in the 2022-23 spring term.
Speaking to the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS) in October, a spokesperson for the council said there was no single reason behind the rise, but parents became more confident in educating their children following the pandemic.
"Some families actively prefer home education because of educational philosophy, flexibility, cultural reasons, religious beliefs, family lifestyle, or a desire for personalised learning," the spokesperson added.
Nazreen, from Hull, worked as an English teacher in secondary schools for 10 years, before leaving in August to tutor from home.
Since January, she has employed other tutors to educate her 14-year-old daughter, Lalia, at home.
She says she made the decision because it was a "struggle" to manage Lalia's competitive tennis commitments alongside school.
"Obviously, with the tennis, she needed more flexibility, but I do feel that schools nowadays can be quite a negative environment," Nazreen says.
She believes pupils are not given enough independence at school, often have multiple supply teachers because of staff shortages, and learning at home allows for a more productive, consistent approach.
"[Lalia] can do so much more in the time given because there's no distractions. What she does in an hour would probably take three hours at school."
She adds: "She just feels like she's in a much more positive environment."
Chris Watts, a former headteacher and school inspector from Woodall Spa, Lincolnshire, says home education "can work", but argues school is about more than "what happens in the classroom".
In particular, he says attending is important for young people's socialisation.
"You don't just have breaks to get breathers," Watts says. "It's a time for children to socialise and the curriculum itself has got socialisation built into it.
"It's about them finding their place in a social context and I think those are building blocks really for their future."
In Lincolnshire, the percentage of children who are home educated rose from 2.3% in 2023-2024 to 2.86% in 2025-2026, according to the county council.
Watts says teachers are good role models for children.
"You'd find it difficult to find a person, never mind a child, who can't identify a significant adult in their life, or a significant teacher."
Dame Rachel de Souza, the children's commissioner, says the majority of parents choosing to take children out of school "have their child's best interest at heart" and "often feel it is a last resort".
However, she has called for "stronger protections" for home-educated children.
The Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026, which came into force in April, established a Not in School register and gave English councils greater powers intervene where they believe a child is not receiving a suitable education.
"But a register alone is not enough," Dame Rachel says. "Councils need the staff, funding and capacity to build relationships with families, provide support for the families who are doing a great job, make the right checks and intervene when a child is at potential risk."

“This topic should not be part of the negotiations,” Kubilius stated when asked whether EU enlargement should become a central issue in peace talks involving Ukraine.
He argued that the EU should make clear to the Russian leader Vladimir Putin that continuing the war will not prevent Ukraine from joining the bloc or halt EU enlargement more broadly. According to Kubilius, Moscow should not be given the ability to block accession, even if the timetable differs between candidate countries, DW wrote.
Kubilius argued that continued enlargement could itself influence Moscow’s calculations. He claimed Putin launched the war partly because he feared that successful development in Ukraine and neighboring countries could encourage Russians to consider alternatives to his rule.
“If we make it clear that enlargement will happen even if the war continues, this could become an additional argument for convincing Moscow to end the war,” Kubilius stated.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos took a more cautious position, noting that it remains unclear whether enlargement will play a role in any future peace agreement. Kos explained that the European Commission’s current task is to advance Ukraine’s gradual integration into the EU and help establish the legal framework required for postwar reconstruction, according to DW.
She also expressed optimism that Ukraine and Moldova could open the final two clusters in their EU accession negotiations in December.
Earlier in November, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas stated that the European Union must be directly involved in any eventual peace agreement concerning Ukraine, including on security guarantees, sanctions, reconstruction, and Ukraine’s integration into the bloc. She added that Russia has no veto over European security arrangements.

Naughty Dog’s Michael Barclay – whose credits include Uncharted: The Lost Legacy and The Last of Us 2 – says he’s “made video games for 19 years and GTA 6 appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child”.
Rockstar’s latest open world release is by far the best-looking game ever made, even if it is locked to 30fps on PS5 hardware .
And it’s being treated like witchcraft by devs, who naturally have a greater appreciation for the feats on display.
Barclay, who’s currently working on next year’s Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet , continued :

“I'm always astonished that [Rockstar’s] environmental lighting is mostly dynamic and looks as good if not better than most baked lighting.”
In really, really simple terms, baked lighting is a game development technique used to save computational cost by calculating light and shadow data in advance.
The downside to this is that it’s fixed, but obviously given the ever-changing nature of GTA 6’s sandbox, it needs to have a dynamic solution.
Barclay is saying that GTA 6’s dynamic lighting matches and even surpasses those pre-determined solutions in many scenarios, making it a real accomplishment.
These comments triggered discussion from various other industry professionals, including Tim Soret from Odd Tales, the makers of The Last Night , who outlined some of his thoughts on the title:
GTA 6 sets a standard so unfathomably high I do wonder at what point it’ll ever be topped.
I suppose raising the bar like this will motivate the many other talented devs around the world, but not every studio will have access to the time and the estimated $1 billion budget that allowed Rockstar to deliver this.
Either way, it’s clear industry professionals are utterly blown away by what the studio has delivered here.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".
Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".
Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.
Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.
Polish Defence Minister WÅadysÅaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said.  Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.
On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister RadosÅaw Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".
"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.

United Nations climate talks in Turkey have approached a final deal as COP31 presidents hope to finally achieve consensus on how to advance the fight against global warming.
COP31 president Murat Kurum told a late-night plenary session: “We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon,” as the conference was set to reconvene on Sunday morning to approve the deal.
To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts warn of the need for urgent and deep cuts to emissions, mainly from the use of coal, oil and gas. The world is already on track to blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperature.
Civil society organisations wrote to Cop31 ’s joint presidents, Australia’s Chris Bowen and Murat Kurum, overnight to tell them they had hours left to avoid making it “one of the most disappointing Cops [the UN] has ever had”.
“The Global South is being abandoned,” they said. “Developed countries have blocked progress across the negotiations and arrived with no new finance commitments.”
Negotiators ran past a Friday deadline, straight through Saturday and into the early hours of Sunday. Their new version of the deal text refined an earlier draft, which had been heavily criticised by some for lacking ambition because it contained no reference to ending the use of fossil fuels.
Kurum has said he felt concerns around fossil fuels had been addressed, as had those around helping developing countries finance their adaptations to climate change.
Delegations have until 3am GMT to raise any objections to the deal, with a session scheduled at 6am GMT to begin approving it.
Australia led the talks with Turkey, which is hosting the meeting, and nearly 200 delegations from the world’s richest, poorest, largest and smallest nations. It was hoped that a year of climate disasters could help sharpen minds at the conference.
Devastating floods in Mozambique flooded more than 150,000 homes and killed at least 22 people. Coming off the back of other climate disasters in the country - including Cyclone Kenneth in 2019, as well as a crippling drought across 2023 and 2024 - charities told The Independent they were struggling to attract donors due to foreign aid cuts.
In August, after a piece of melting glacier dislodged high up in the mountains, devastating floods in Nepal caused an estimated $4.8bn in damages, and left 1,500 dead and 10,000 injured.
There is also the threat a record breaking El Nino weather event that the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) has projected that an additional 49 million more people could be pushed into hunger globally.
A climate “loss and damage” fund was established at Cop27 in Egypt in 2022 in order to provide developing countries with compensation for climate disasters. But it has so far secured just $822m in pledges, and countries affected by climate disasters are limited to apply for only $20m per disaster – less than half a per cent of Nepal’s needs.
“Nepal did not create the climate problem. But we keep being hit by massive floods, not just this year but also in 2025, 2022 and other years,” said Bisesh Sangat, a Nepali attendee of Cop31 who works for the NGO Practical Action. “There’s a lot of big infrastructure losses, but also the human losses mean that you go to villages and there are lots of widows and children without fathers, so the losses are very profound.”
There was already deep disappointment after a draft published on Thursday afternoon failed to include any mention of fossil fuels - despite the fact that this had previously been mentioned in the outcome of Cop28 in Dubai in 2023.
This cover decision is seen as the key outcome of the UN climate conference, and is set to be a key signal that countries will take home and implement in national policy.
Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank said: "If this version of the text remains, it will be a ghost COP. The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here. After the progress made in 2023 at Cop28 in Dubai where fossil fuels were mentioned for the first time, there is now no mention of the f-word at all. Cop31 has been muzzled on the most important threat causing the climate crisis."
Stories emerging from the negotiating room suggest that the usual suspects were to blame for an outcome that was less ambitious than hoped. Saudi Arabia has been among the main objectors to any wording on the “transition away from fossil fuels”, with insiders suggesting that the world’s largest oil exporter played a key role in blocking ambitious language.
Pelin Zorlu, senior research fellow lead on climate and energy at the Chatham House think tank, said: “The Cop Presidency has acknowledged the difficulty of reaching consensus on fossil fuels, with opposition from the Arab Group, Russia and others.”
But others pointed their fingers at the EU for not being ambitious enough, particularly around Turkey’s high profile pledge to raise electricity's share of total final energy consumption from around 23 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035. Such a move makes sense if the electricity is powered by renewables – but not if it is done so with coal.
Laurie van der Burg, from NGO Oil Change International, said: “The EU is trying to shift blame onto others and it is deeply hypocritical. At the beginning of Cop31, it signalled it was prepared to drop the renewable energy sources ask from the electrification target and it has failed to put forward an EU fossil fuel transition roadmap. Even worse, the EU blocked progress on the public finance, adaptation, and just transition that developing countries urgently need. These are not side issues. They are essential to making a fair fossil fuel phaseout possible and protecting communities from climate disasters.”
At the same time, the EU and other wealthy democracies have expressed dismay at receiving too much blame when it is they who are providing the bulk of climate finance - and especially so with the US absent. EU member states provided €32.3bn in public “climate finance” in 2025, which mobilised a further €9.3bn in private finance.
There is growing disquiet that the group of countries who are required to provide this “climate finance” – crucial capital needed to decarbonise and adapt to climate change – is fixed around a list of developed countries that was devised in 1992, known as “Annex II”. It means that newly-wealthy countries, including China, the UAE, South Korea and Singapore, do not officially have to provide climate finance, while the likes of Greece and Portugal are required to.
While plenty of lobbyists were in attendance, one group was conspicuously absent: world leaders. Neither China’s Xi Jinping or India’s Narendra Modi, or any hint of the US federal government made an appearance – with Andy Burnham the only G7 leader in attendance. Yet, while powerful countries fight it out, ultimately it is the world’s most climate vulnerable countries who are losing out.
On Friday afternoon, Ghana's minister for environment, science and technology, Dr Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings did not mince her words.
Africans were being “excluded by the use of technicalities, with the use of inaccessible finance, and with the use of shifting goalposts and lack of commitment and delivery on promises… Africa is not a continent merely seeking assistance. We are asking the developed countries to keep promises that they already made.”
In what seemed to be a reference to the US, she said: “There are countries who from the onset decided not to be a part of this agreement. There, they were plain and honest… What we do not appreciate are those who choose to remain a part of the framewor

articles.title_orig: These iPhone Customizations Can Make Your Lock Screen Look Cooler
articles.title_zh: These iPhone Customizations Can Make Your Lock Screen Look Cooler
articles.content_orig:
Over the past few years, Apple has improved how much users can customize their iPhone Lock Screen. Initially, the company only allowed changes to the background wallpaper. Then, how it showed wallpaper when the screen dimmed. Now, the lock screen works with customization widgets, allowing you to add and change many aspects of what the iPhone's Lock Screen can do . You could tweak the clock, the wallpaper, fonts, and add color filters. Suddenly, there were widgets and Live Activities too. The latest iOS 27 update, which comes with the all-new Siri AI, also included more customizations to the clock and widgets, allowing you to make the iPhone look more your own.
Interestingly enough, Apple's great revamp on iPhone customization started with iOS 18 , which coincides with the moment the company should've made available all the Apple Intelligence features we are only seeing now. The company had already begun offering ways to change the lock screen with widgets, filters, and new fonts. With iOS 18, Apple added those features to the Home Screen, and Control Center, while making more refinements to the lock screen too.
After that, Apple brought the Liquid Glass design language with iOS 26, which gave the iPhone's software a visual overhaul. As of 2026, Apple's included improvements like animated album covers from Apple Music on the Lock Screen, access to up to three Live Activities in the Dynamic Island, and more.
All that change is a lot to keep track of. So here's an easy list of the best ways you can customize your iPhone Lock Screen to look cooler.
If you're running iOS 27 and have access to the new set of Apple Intelligence features thanks to the new Siri AI, one of the coolest things you can do is to extend your wallpaper on the Lock Screen. For example, if you have the perfect photo, but it's in landscape orientation, or you don't want your partner's or pet's face too zoomed in on your Lock Screen, here's what you can do: After long pressing the Lock Screen > Adding/Customizing a Lock Screen , you can zoom out the image until the iPhone gets an "Extend" feature. Using on-device AI, the iPhone will recreate a part of the image to make it fit the vibe you're going for.
Once you do that, you can customize other parts of your Lock Screen. If you have an iPhone with the Action Button and Camera Control functionalities, for example, you can remove the traditional Flashlight and Camera widgets to something else you might want to access faster, if these options are redundant to you. There's a number of shortcuts you can choose from, including Apple options and third-party apps. Et voilà, you have the most original Lock Screen possible.
Another cool feature introduced with iOS 27 is the opposite of what previous software brought. While the Lock Screen clock was getting bigger over the years, now you can make it smaller to give it a very minimal aesthetic look. Just tap on the clock while editing, and then on the upper right of the font options is a button that looks like two rectangles. Tap it, and your clock will shrink into the date area.
Another important tweak that few people actually take advantage of is Apple's Focus Modes. Introduced in 2021's iOS 15 update , Apple lets you create different Lock Screen, Home Screen, wallpapers, and filters for different parts of your day or mood. You can create one for work, and another for while you're in the car. If you're at swim practice, you can set another wallpaper and only allow specific people to call you, etc.
Mastering Focus Mode can take a while because it has so many potential combinations of its features, but the outcome can be very rewarding. Many people use it to avoid getting those endless social media notifications during work hours, or even prevent Trello and Slack from buzzing you when you're long gone from your work. Did I mention these Focus Modes can be set up by location? Since your phone knows where you are, the Focus Modes can trigger when you get to or leave a specific place, by a specific hour, or even when Apple Intelligence understands you're doing something else — like when you start playing a game or commuting on the bus.
You can find Focus Modes by opening the Control Center and venturing inside the Focus tab. With that, you can go beyond the Do Not Disturb option and create different filters for the day, including unique Lock Screen combinations that make sense for that specific moment of the day.
Another cool feature for someone who wants a completely different Lock Screen wallpaper is to create AI-generated wallpapers based on your photos, or memoji, or even just a prompt you give about a visual you're imagining in your head. When customizing a Lock Screen , tap the Plus button , then Image Playground , select between a few design styles, and then describe an image for a unique wallpaper. A bonus tip is that with iOS 27, you can even remove the Now Playing card from the Lock Screen, and whatever is playing will continue to play, bringing the ultimate minimalist design.

articles.title_orig: Trump opens door to bipartisan deal on credit card rates as Americans face record debt

articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump joins 'Saturday in America' to discuss the recent FBI hack, bipartisanship and his recent trip to China.
President Donald Trump signaled Saturday that he is willing to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10%, renewing his push to lower borrowing costs as Americans grapple with record credit card debt.
During an interview with Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany on "Saturday in America," Trump was asked whether he could work with Democrats in the next session of Congress to establish a one-year cap.
"I would do it," Trump responded. "These credit card companies have made a lot and the credit card fees that they charge, I'm all into it."
Trump acknowledged that some critics could view the proposed cap as inconsistent with free-market principles, but argued that consumers should not face excessive fees.
AS US CREDIT CARD DEBT HITS $1.29T, BANK ALGORITHMS ARE REJECTING DEBT-FREE, SIX-FIGURE EARNERS
President Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10%, arguing that credit card companies are charging Americans excessive interest and fees. (Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters / Reuters)
"I know that some people would say it's not free enterprise, but what's free enterprise when you're sitting home and you get a bill that some guy set up in an office on Park Avenue and they said, 'let's charge a fee that's too high,'" he continued. "So I'm all for that."
Trump added, "The credit card companies, they're getting too much, the fees are too high and the interests are too high."
The president's comments come as nationwide credit card balances have soared to a record $1.29 trillion — a 67% surge since early 2021, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
Trump previously called for a one-year cap limiting credit card interest rates to 10% in a Truth Social post in January.
MAMDANI THANKS TRUMP FOR HELPING SMALL BUSINESSES IN NYC, NATIONWIDE: 'PRESIDENT HAS DELIVERED RELIEF'
U.S. credit card balances have climbed to a record $1.29 trillion, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, as President Donald Trump renews his push to cap interest rates. (iStock / iStock)
He argued at the time that the Biden administration had allowed rates to rise as high as 20% to 30% and that Americans were being "ripped off" by credit card companies.
Trump's renewed interest in the cap drew support from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, including Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., who has previously introduced legislation to cap credit card interest rates.
"The President is right. Let's pass my bill to cap credit card interest fees," Hawley wrote on X.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., also welcomed Trump's remarks.
TRUMP ADMIN POURING $480M LOAN INTO GULF OF AMERICA OIL AND GAS PROJECT
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., welcomed President Donald Trump's support for limiting credit card interest rates, calling on lawmakers to approve a cap to save Americans money. (Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Protect Borrowers / Getty Images)
"Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money," Warren posted on X in response to Trump's interview.
Major banking industry organizations have warned that imposing a 10% cap could limit access to credit, particularly for consumers with lower credit scores.
In a joint statement earlier this year, several banking associations warned that the proposal could force lenders to reduce credit availability and push borrowers toward more expensive alternatives, calling the cap "devastating" for millions of Americans.

Despite opposition from the banking industry, Trump's proposal could receive renewed attention when Democrats take control of Congress in January, with several lawmakers already expressing support for limiting credit card interest rates.

Ferrari unveiled the 296 Challenge Stradale and 296 Challenge EVO, two new cars developed in close collaboration to highlight the symbiotic bond between the Prancing Horse's race cars and production cars, as well as the exceptionally high level of technology transfer that sets them apart. The 296 Challenge EVO builds on the car that redefined the standards of the Ferrari Challenge and will make its debut in the 2027 season, while the 296 Challenge Stradale brings the technical essence and pursuit of uncompromising performance to a road-legal vehicle.
The cars were unveiled during the 2026 Ferrari Finali Mondiali, held at the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya in Montmeló. The final event of the Prancing Horse's racing season brings together, on the same track, the Ferrari Challenge, programmes dedicated to competition cars and non-competitive activities.
The 296 Challenge Stradale is the Ferrari currently in the range that can offer the most direct link to a race car. The car is indeed stripped-back, almost clinical in its setup, entirely geared towards providing the driver with a direct and physical driving experience. Performance, consistency, and repeatability of driving characteristics thus become the defining characteristics of its dynamic setup.
The 296 Challenge EVO, on the other hand, builds on the strengths of the 296 Challenge with the aim of boosting absolute performance without compromising driveability and consistency. The versatile aerodynamic package, improved dynamic controls, and wider operating range make the car faster, more predictable, and more consistent, bringing the driving experience even closer to that of the 296 GT3 Evo.
Both feature the 2,992 cc 120° Ferrari twin-turbo V6 engine in the exclusively internal-combustion configuration of the 296 Speciale, which has received numerous accolades and rewritten lap records at circuits throughout Europe. In the 296 Challenge Stradale, it develops 670 hp at 8,000 rpm and is paired with an eight-speed dual-clutch F1 transmission; in the 296 Challenge EVO, it instead delivers 700 hp at 7,500 rpm, with a specific output of 234 hp/l and a seven-speed F1 transmission. The absence of a hybrid component limits the car's weight and complexity, further underscoring the direct connection between driver and accelerator, engine, and rear wheels.
The 296 Challenge Stradale has a dry weight of 1,330 kg, a full 140 kg less than the 296 GTB, and boasts a weight-to-power ratio of 1.98 kg/hp. The 296 Challenge EVO shares the same weight, underscoring the fact that both cars have been designed with a focus on lightweight construction and performance.
This approach is also evident in the design. The volumes and surfaces of the Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale have been stripped of superfluous elements to reduce the car's visual mass and make its technical functions more readily apparent. The result is a deliberately more essential and racing-inspired design language, in which every element serves a purpose and helps distinguish it from the other berlinettas in the range. The car thus retains its visual connection with the 296 Challenge EVO, reinterpreting it in line with the safety, type-approval, and practical requirements specific to a road car.
Aerodynamics represent one of the principal points of contact between the two cars: the 296 Challenge Stradale generates 617 kg of downforce at 250 km/h, 72% more than the 296 GTB, through an integrated system comprising a fixed rear wing, splitter, flick, aero damper, vortex generators, and a fully enclosed underbody.
The 296 Challenge EVO increases maximum downforce by 12% compared with the 296 Challenge, equivalent to an additional 100 kg at 250 km/h, and introduces the Low Drag configuration, which reduces minimum drag by 4%. The difference in aerodynamic load between the High Downforce and Low Drag setups has more than doubled. The wider wing adjustment range, the Low Drag kit, the redesigned rear diffuser, the new mirrors, and the carbon-fibre components extend the 296 Challenge EVO's operating window across different circuits. A high-performance driveshaft with dedicated cooling broadens the component's operating window under the most demanding conditions. The option to increase rear ride height by up to 10 mm provides approximately 30 kg of additional downforce at 250 km/h.
The vehicle's dynamics follow the same philosophy of maximising performance. The 296 Challenge Stradale features ABS Evo in all driving conditions and in every Manettino setting, along with specific control systems, a dedicated setup, and Pirelli P Zero R and P Zero Trofeo RS tyres. The 296 Challenge EVO updates its traction-control and electronic-differential control strategies to improve combined performance, braking stability, and agility through high-speed corners; the new brake-pedal curve also increases modulation, travel, and pedal load at the same level of deceleration.
The 296 Challenge EVO improves consistency over race distances and reduces tyre degradation. In comparative testing, the car proved faster on the circuits analysed, with an improvement of 0.8 seconds at Mugello compared with the 296 Challenge. The redesigned instrument cluster makes driving information, control intervention levels, TPMS data and lap times easier to read. These features are particularly significant in the run-up to 2027, when the Ferrari Challenge will introduce three rounds featuring 40-minute Endurance races, beginning with the second event of the season at Mugello, which will mark the debut of the new format.
The engine retains the 120° twin-turbo V6 architecture in the 'hot-V' configuration first introduced on the 296 GTB. On the 296 Challenge Stradale, the concept has been further developed in full line with the racing development philosophy: there is no hybrid component, and the engine, turbocharging system, and transmission have been developed with direct reference to the 296 Challenge. Maximum power is 670 hp at 8,000 rpm. Optimising boost pressure and cam phasers improves low-end response and reduces time to boost. articles.title_orig: What to Do Now to Prepare for the Next Bank Outage
articles.title_zh: What to Do Now to Prepare for the Next Bank Outage
articles.content_orig:
Customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, U.S. Bank and other major financial institutions reported service outages on Monday, according to Downdetector.com .
Other banks that saw a spike in customer complaints about difficulty accessing their accounts included Capital One, Truist and Wells Fargo, while users also reported problems with the digital payments app Zelle, according to the outage tracker.
However, Downdetector showed that service was back to normal at the banks and Zelle early Tuesday.
CBS News has reached out for comment to Chase, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Capital One.
Bank of America told CBS News in a statement that its "systems were operating normally throughout the day yesterday."
Chase Bank's services were experiencing a technical bug issue, not a cyber issue, a spokesperson said Monday.
"Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," a Chase spokesperson said in a statement. "We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible."
Chase also said in a social media post that a software bug in its systems affected other institutions "when we were party to a transaction involving other banks." The issue is not systemic, the bank added.
Some Chase customers received a message that said, "Some services aren't available. We're working on them. Please try back later."
Bank customers started reporting problems accessing online services on Monday morning. By the afternoon, reports of outages had surged, according to Downdetector.com. As of 2 p.m. ET, nearly 4,800 users had reported problems with Chase, the most of any bank.
Chase customers reported issues accessing their online accounts, including viewing balances and performing transactions such as bank transfers and wire transfers, according to Downdetector.
Bank of America clients reported problems with ATMs as well as online and mobile banking services, according to the outage tracker. A Bank of America spokesperson told CBS News its "systems have been operating normally today."
U.S. Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app. They also had problems transferring funds, while Wells Fargo customers reported difficulty signing in to their accounts, as well as with getting account balances and conducting transactions.
A Chase Bank customer in Texas told CBS News he tried to deposit a check at a Dallas branch early Monday, but the transaction could not be completed. A bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" without providing additional details, he added, expressing frustration at the lack of clarity about the situation.
A spokesperson for U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly impacted by the cyber outage. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the company said in a statement to CBS News.
A Capital One spokesperson said it hasn't been affected by the outage and continues to operate normally.
Zelle told CBS News its service was "operating as it should," but that some users could be experiencing issues related to problems at their financial institutions, which could be delaying Zelle payments.
"Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds," a Zelle spokesperson said. "Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds."
Zelle's network operator, Early Warning Services, is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.
The banking outages occurred after Microsoft restored services on Saturday following a global outage affecting its Outlook and Teams services, which disrupted users, companies and government operations worldwide. Microsoft said a technical issue caused the outage and that it was not linked to a cyberattack.
The glitches also came only days after overloaded routers forced the Federal Aviation Administration to order a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday, stranding travelers and causing thousands of canceled flights. The FAA said Sunday that airline schedules across the U.S. were returning to normal . (On Monday evening, United Airlines also said it resolved a " widespread system outage " it had been dealing with that afternoon.)
Cybersecurity experts said the root causes of the bank service disruptions, Microsoft outage and FAA system failure, while different on their face, also point to a common problem.
"Our country has seen three very serious technology incidents over the past week," Mike Chapple, an IT, analytics and operations expert at the University of Notre Dame, said in a statement to CBS News. "When we dig into the details, each one has an explanation that makes sense on its own, but they all point to a common theme: the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day."
He noted that in each case, a technical issue quickly rippled through interconnected systems, causing massive disruptions nationwide.
"We don't yet know much about today's banking system outage, but it appears to stem from a technical issue at Chase that affected other banks through their shared payment networks," Chapple added.
When big companies like JPMorgan Chase experience technical disruptions, their impact often reverberates industrywide, added Karen Panetta, dean of graduate engineering at Tufts University.
"The larger companies have global reach that affords their customers flexibility and seamless integration with other businesses," she told CBS News. "Unfortunately, when one of these backbone providers has disruptions, the downstream effects are magnified. The multiple entities that rely on those services are also affected."
Kayne McGladrey, a security expert and senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, said bank customers might have better luck going to their local branch in person, noting that financial services often still work on site when online banking resources go down.
"Try ATMs, cards, phone banking and branches, which often keep working when the app doesn't," he said in a statement to CBS News.
He also advised people to keep records of any attempted or failed transactions.
"Screenshot failed transactions and error messages, since you may need them for reconciliation or fee waivers. Once service is back, ask the bank to reverse any fees the outage caused," McGladrey said.
He also urged consumers to ignore unsolicited emails about the bank outages, which she warned might be phishing scams. Instead, people should rely on their bank's official communication channels for information, McGladrey said.
Craig Timm, senior director of anti-money laundering at ACAMS, an anti-financial-crime organization, told CBS News he expects criminals to exploit consumer anxiety about potentially losing access to their money, and that consumers should "assume they will be targeted." That's in part because AI lets scammers act fast and at scale.
Timm said common tactics to be alert to include criminals exerting pressure on targets "to take urgent action to protect their funds or restore account access."
"These scams may take the form of fake bank alerts, phishing texts or emails, or social media posts that claim to offer help," he said. "Some schemes aim to steal banking login credentials, while others use malicious links to gain access to a victim's computer."

Nvidia's ongoing AI chip controversy has just taken another unexpected turn. This time around, Chinese tech giant Alibaba appears to be part of the story. A new investigation claims Nvidia's very own sales team helped connect Alibaba with a businesswoman whose companies would later come under scrutiny for allegedly smuggling billions of dollars' worth of restricted AI chips into China.
According to The Information , Nvidia employees introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang on two occasions over several months in 2022. The report, citing three people with direct knowledge of the matter, says these introductions happened before the United States imposed major export restrictions on advanced Nvidia semiconductors.
The connections reportedly went on to help Huang establish Alibaba as a customer for her emerging chip-rental business. This would later create an opportunity that would prove valuable as Washington tightened its restrictions on advanced AI hardware.
The Information reports that securing Alibaba as a customer helped Huang's company obtain bank loans to finance purchases of servers equipped with Nvidia chips. After Huang became a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company, it began offering customers access to Nvidia's powerful AI hardware through data centers in Southeast Asia.
This business model was convenient for Chinese companies who were unable to purchase certain Nvidia processors directly. Now, they could potentially rent access to computing power hosted outside China. However, renting cloud computing resources is distinct from physically smuggling restricted chips across borders.
The report adds that a corporate network linked to Huang, including Megaspeed and Shanghai Century Litong, allegedly moved billions of dollars' worth of restricted Nvidia hardware into China between 2023 and 2025. This new investigation raises questions about how Nvidia's sales relationships helped that network develop. Even so, it doesn't directly establish that the company knowingly facilitated illegal exports.
The allegations arrive amid growing scrutiny of Nvidia's business relationships in Asia and the recent departure of its longtime CEO, Jensen Huang , following a separate controversy involving Alice Huang. On November 16, the US Departments of Justice and Commerce confirmed that investigators began examining Megaspeed for potential export-control violations in 2024.
Authorities requested Nvidia's sales records in May 2025, and the company placed Megaspeed on its internal no-sell list the following month. The Justice Department subsequently took the lead in the criminal investigation.
Neither Nvidia's introductions nor Alibaba's reported customer relationship independently establishes wrongdoing. Meanwhile, Megaspeed has maintained that it complies with applicable laws, and investigators have not publicly established that Alibaba participated in illegal chip shipments.

articles.title_zh: Trump says he'd work with Dems to cap credit card interest, fees
articles.content_orig:

NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates , hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.
"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."
Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers . The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.
Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House's affordability push . Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.
The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Trump's promise.
That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates.
In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money."
Other Democrats have endorsed the idea in various ways, including Rep. Maxine Waters of California, a powerful Democrat who sits on the House Financial Services Committee. Among Republicans, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri has proposed several caps on credit card interest rates, as recently as this year when Trump made his proposal.
"The President is right. Let's pass my bill to cap credit card interest fees," Hawley posted on X on Saturday.
Researchers who studied Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.
About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.
Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

articles.title_orig: UN climate talk negotiators go into second day of overtime while at odds over fossil fuels
articles.title_zh: UN climate talk negotiators go into second day of overtime while at odds over fossil fuels
articles.content_orig:
Talks were set to resume at the UN COP31 summit on Sunday for a second day of overtime as countries struggle to reach a new global climate deal.
Nations were deadlocked in Turkey on how to advance the fight against global warming, after new draft agreements included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
A third and "final" text was sent to delegates in the early hours of Sunday morning and members had until 06:00 local time (0300 GMT) to raise concerns before a 9am local time (0600GMT) meeting for approval.
If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended to reconvene next year.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.
The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday . On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.
As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.
COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates in the early hours of Sunday morning he believed concerns had been addressed.
"We ask you to look at this decision carefully," Kurum said.
"We are closer than ever to agreement on the remaining issues."
If the countries can't agree, the summit would end with no deal and be reconvened next year.
This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU were fighting to have a commitment to move away from fossil fuels put back into the final agreement, after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
Tuvalu's Climate Minister Maina Talia told reporters it was a "red line" for the low-lying Pacific nation: "We're talking about the root cause of all of this".
France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture - a technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground.
She said it was being used as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
For the first time at a COP, the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal set under the Paris climate accord of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
But Australia's Climate Change and Energy Minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.
He argued the summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
Another key issues raised by developing nations is the the lack of money.
Another sticking point involved a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptations to climate change, however the EU has previously said it would not support this.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - a figure that was then removed.
"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.
